Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- **Registry drift.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py crosswalk` (`portfolio_json` is in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`). It compares `portfolio.json` with every DEV folder and Drive `01_PROJECTS` folder and only reports; it never moves anything. Do not fix drift during closeout. List each item it found under "Still open", naming any folder created this session first: that is a project started without a row, the exact way projects got lost before the 2026-10-03 organization pass. `drive_unreachable` means the Drive checks never ran; say so, do not call it clean. Cowork cannot run it; say it was skipped.
- **7-day rule.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply`. Name any project it paused, and any project on its last two days, under "Still open" with what it still needs (a receiver, step 1). Revive with the board's status pill or `portfolio.py` once there is a first step to show.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- **Registry edits get their own commit.** In project-triage, if `git status --porcelain portfolio.json` shows a change (board edits from the day, `set-status`, `set-receiver`), commit that file alone first as `data: board edits <YYYY-MM-DD>`, then the rest. The board header's "N unpushed registry edits" counts these; a skipped one becomes a JSON merge conflict when the other machine edits too.
- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- If `~/.claude/mods` changed this session (a mod added, edited or `.disabled`), run the mods sync (`bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` on the Mac, `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\mods\mods-sync.ps1` on Windows) and list any invalid mod under "Still open".
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours. On a Cowork-only day it may be absent; say so, it is not an error.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first. Item 1 is one concrete action (a command to run or a file to open), not a theme: it is the line `~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py` shows Eric the next morning
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

**Keep the resume cards true (PM system design Decision 9).** The live board shows each project as a card read from STATUS and the registry; if a card doesn't make sense tonight, it won't in six weeks. Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py scan --days 1` (about a minute), then `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py card-check`. It prints the card of every registry project touched today, on either machine, with its gaps. Fix each gap before the Step 2 commit:

- `STATUS has no entry dated <today>`: add `- <today>: <what happened>` under the repo's Done / Current state.
- `STATUS has no Next item`: put one concrete action first under `## Next`.
- `no next step (next_action)` (Drive-only row): set it on the board or with `portfolio.py add-update <name> "<note>" --next-action "<step>"`.
- `needs a receiver`: `portfolio.py set-receiver <name> "<who>"` (a name, or `me: <why>`). Ask Eric when it is not obvious from the session; never invent one.
- `touched but marked <status>`: revive it (`portfolio.py set-status <name> active`) or say in STATUS why a retired project was touched.

Re-run `card-check` after the fixes. Its output is the last section of the report (**Cards:**); trim to projects with work today if it is long, but never drop one that still has a gap.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Registry drift:** <N items, or "none"> (`portfolio.py crosswalk`)
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.

**Cards:** <`portfolio.py card-check` output, after the Step 4 fixes>
```

The cards come last on purpose: they are what the next session, on either machine, picks up from.

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

**Where everything landed.** Build that list from the ledger, not from memory: the Step 4 `landed.py scan --days 1` already refreshed it (it reads git in every DEV repo and file times on Drive and the vault, so files written by scripts and shell copies are included); run `landed.py show --days 1`. Put its project-grouped output in the report under **Landed:** (trim to the projects this session touched if it is long). The ledger lives in `~/.claude/global-memory/landed/` and is pushed with global-memory, so `/landed` on the other machine shows it too.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
definition.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
definition.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. SecondBrain Queue is the priority lane; promotion eligibility is controlled by promotion_scope.

4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- articulation-skill: Help users explain complex ideas simply to non-technical audiences with proven communication frameworks. Use when users need to explain technical concepts, structure presentations or writing, create clear documentation, improve communication clarity, or translate jargon into accessible language. Triggers include requests like "help me explain this clearly", "how do I structure this presentation", "make this less technical", "help me articulate this idea", or any request to simplify complex communication. Do not use for building a slide deck (use five-slides-generator or research-in-5) or for light copyediting of text that is already clear.
- ArXiv
- backup
- brain-audit
- capture-insight
- claude-stack-doctor: Health-check Eric's automation/memory stack in one pass and verify the Mac-to-Windows handoff works: launchd agents / Windows scheduled tasks, Python venvs, memsearch, the memory-compiler flush pipeline, backup freshness, and context budget. Use when the user says "/claude-stack-doctor", "stack doctor", "is my stack healthy", "did my scheduled jobs run", "check the memory pipeline", "why didn't the backup run", or when closeout/morning sessions should verify automation health. Do not use to run the backup itself (use backup) or to audit context-engineering practice (use doctor-plus).
- closeout
- decision-audit: Decision Drain Audit: sort the decisions Eric has been avoiding into four buckets (decide now, needs one piece of information, waiting on someone, not mine), name why they are stuck, give 3 tiny next actions, then optionally decide them and record each answer where it lives. Use when the user says "/decision-audit", "decision drain audit", "what decisions am I avoiding", "what's stuck", "fill out my pending decisions", or "let's work through the decisions". Do not use for the Friday synthesis (use weekly-review), ranking projects (use project), or the biweekly report (use status-report).
- dev-sync
- doctor-plus
- fireflies-intake: One-command Fireflies pipeline — sync new meeting transcripts into the SecondBrain vault, rename generically-titled meetings, then report exactly what was ingested. Use when the user says "/fireflies-intake", "ingest my recent fireflies meetings", "sync meetings that aren't in the second brain yet", "pull in the new meetings", "meeting ingestion", or asks whether all recent meetings have been ingested. Do not use to search what was said in transcripts (use pp-fireflies).
- five-slides-generator
- forecast-capture
- graphify: Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. Turns any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) into a persistent knowledge graph with god nodes, community detection, and query/path/explain tools. Do not use for a quick lookup of one known file or symbol, or for sport-science literature questions (use sports-science-research-grounding).
- grill-with-ui: Run a grilling interview on a local browser page instead of the terminal. Every question is laid out with its recommendation, answerable in any order, with a per-question discussion thread and one "Send to Agent" button. Use when the user says "grill with ui", invokes /grill-with-ui with a topic, or says "/grill-with-ui resume".
- harvest
- html-to-pdf: Render any local HTML report, deck, or dashboard to a print-ready PDF via headless Chrome — replaces the manual Ctrl+P → Save as PDF ritual. Use when the user says "export this to PDF", "print version", "PDF for the coaches", "make this printable", or a coach-facing HTML deliverable needs a shareable/printable copy. Do not use to build the report or deck itself (use status-report or five-slides-generator).
- humanizer: Remove signs of AI-generated writing from text. Use when editing or reviewing
text to make it sound more natural and human-written. Based on Wikipedia's
comprehensive "Signs of AI writing" guide. Detects and fixes patterns including:
inflated symbolism, promotional language, superficial -ing analyses, vague
attributions, em dash overuse, rule of three, AI vocabulary words, negative
parallelisms, and excessive conjunctive phrases.
- impeccable: Use when the user wants to design, redesign, shape, critique, audit, polish, clarify, distill, harden, optimize, adapt, animate, colorize, extract, or otherwise improve a frontend interface. Covers websites, landing pages, dashboards, product UI, app shells, components, forms, settings, onboarding, and empty states. Handles UX review, visual hierarchy, information architecture, cognitive load, accessibility, performance, responsive behavior, theming, anti-patterns, typography, fonts, spacing, layout, alignment, color, motion, micro-interactions, UX copy, error states, edge cases, i18n, and reusable design systems or tokens. Also use for bland designs that need to become bolder or more delightful, loud designs that should become quieter, live browser iteration on UI elements, or ambitious visual effects that should feel technically extraordinary. Not for backend-only or non-UI tasks.

- context-mode:context-mode: Use context-mode tools (ctx_execute, ctx_execute_file) instead of Bash/cat when processing

- context-mode:ctx-doctor: Run context-mode diagnostics. Checks runtimes, hooks, FTS5,

Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").

While auto mode is active:

You can do much of your work through the Bash tool when it is the simpler route: read files with cat, head, or sed -n, search with grep and find, and make small, mechanical file changes with sed, heredocs, or short scripts instead of the dedicated Read, Edit, or Write tools. # Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive.

**Session routine.** When working inside a project repo, follow the Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` and read `docs/STATUS.md` at the start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, and `git push` at the end. This is what keeps the two machines in step.

# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), finish with the produced file in hand. Check what exists first, then build the file even when a similar one already exists.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.

# Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
